clue.text: Showing dictionary to be in error

indicators.note: letters that are in error are wrongly placed, so the word dictionary must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone shows that a dictionary has got something wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be in error' tells you to rearrange the letters of DICTIONARY, which happen to make exactly the ten letters needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something indicatory points out or signals, so it is showing or indicating.

clue.text: One fled the country

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
ran means fled

explanation.surface: Someone ran away from their homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a refugee; 'the country' is the definition, not the place left.
explanation.definitionFit: Iran is a nation in the Middle East.

clue.text: Many a leftist goes around sick and bored

parts.note: D is the Roman numeral for 500, a crossword sense of many

indicators.note: one piece goes around another, so the word for leftist surrounds the word for sick

parts.note: a Red is a communist, a left-winger
ill means sick

explanation.surface: A good number of left-wingers fall ill and become weary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bored' looks like weariness, but it is the past of bore, to drill a hole. D is 500, a large number.
explanation.definitionFit: Drilled means made a hole in, as bored does in the sense of tunnelling through.

clue.text: "There's no art to find the mind's in the face." (Macbeth)

definitions.text: "There's no art to find the mind's in the face." (Macbeth)

parts.words: There's no art to find the mind's in the face
parts.note: a line from Macbeth with one word missing, filled by the word Duncan uses for how the mind is put together

explanation.walkthrough: King Duncan says this of the traitor Cawdor in Act 1 of Macbeth: the missing word means how a mind is built.
explanation.definitionFit: Duncan's line in Macbeth says you cannot read the make-up of a person's mind from their face.

clue.text: He will have designs on those who patronize him

definitions.text: He will have designs on those who patronize him

parts.words: He will have designs on those who patronize him
parts.note: sounds like a schemer plotting against his patrons, but means someone who inks pictures onto the skin of his customers

explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo artist puts designs on the bodies of his clients, the people who patronize him.

clue.text: Cross about the heartless getting well-established

indicators.note: one piece goes about another, surrounding it, so the cross word wraps the rest

parts.note: a rood is a cross or crucifix in a church

indicators.note: a heartless word loses its middle, leaving only the first and last letters of the

explanation.surface: Someone grumpy about the unfeeling becomes firmly settled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like an adjective, angry, but it is ROOD; 'heartless' removes the H from THE, leaving TE inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rooted has put down roots and is firmly fixed in place.

clue.text: Record absorbing a quiet European

indicators.note: a record absorbing something takes it inside, so the other letters go within

parts.note: LP is a long-playing record
P is piano, the musical direction for quiet

explanation.surface: A gramophone record swallows a hushed person from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'absorbing' puts A and P (piano, quiet) inside LP, the long-playing record.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lapp is a native of Lapland in far northern Europe, now usually called a Sami person.

clue.text: Stylish celebration turned into a game

indicators.note: one piece goes into another, so the reversed party word sits within the rest

parts.note: game in the sense of a lame leg: a game leg is crippled

indicators.note: turned means turned round, so the word for a party is read backwards

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A fashionable party became a sporting contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'game' is not a sport but an adjective, as in a game leg, so it is LAME; 'turned' makes OD from DO.
explanation.definitionFit: A la mode is French for in the fashion, so it means fashionable.

clue.text: Appeals with an attempt to make a joke

parts.note: pleas are appeals or requests
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Earnest requests along with an effort at humour.
explanation.definitionFit: A pleasantry is a light, humorous remark, a little jest.

clue.text: A story told by people can lead to estrangement

parts.note: a story can mean a fib, an untruth
a nation is a people sharing one country

explanation.surface: A tale spread by gossiping folk can drive people apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'story' is used in its childish sense of a lie; 'told by' and 'can lead to' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Estrangement and alienation are synonyms for being made unfriendly or cut off from others.

clue.text: Not well done, so are put to right

indicators.note: one piece is put next to another, so right is placed before the word are

explanation.surface: Steak not cooked through, so it is returned to be corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed solution's P is a misreading of R. 'put to' sets R (right) beside ARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Meat cooked rare is lightly seared, the opposite of well done.

clue.text: The odd train can pass this station

indicators.note: odd means strange or out of order, so the letters of train can pass are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange train is able to go straight through this railway terminus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges TRAIN CAN PASS. St Pancras is a major London railway terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: St Pancras is a London railway station, the terminus for Eurostar and lines to the north.

clue.text: Even a little too low

definitions.meaning: even here means level or smooth, as a surface is
in music a note sung slightly below pitch is said to be this

explanation.surface: A level surface that sits slightly too low.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed solution's P is a misreading of F. In music, a note pitched a little low is flat.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat means level, and in music it describes a note pitched slightly under the true one.

clue.text: Musical drama high-spots for the workers

parts.note: an opera is a drama set to music
tors are rocky hilltops, high points in a landscape

explanation.surface: An opera's climactic moments are staged for the benefit of the workforce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high-spots' looks like climaxes of the opera, but it means tors, rocky hilltops such as those on Dartmoor.
explanation.definitionFit: Operators are people who work machines or run processes, so they are workers.

clue.text: They manipulate people to their advantage

definitions.text: They manipulate people to their advantage

parts.words: They manipulate people to their advantage
parts.note: sounds like exploiters using others, but means practitioners who manipulate bones and joints for the patient's benefit

explanation.definitionFit: Osteopaths treat patients by physically moving and massaging their joints and muscles.

clue.text: An old Jew a cleric and copper backed — held in regard

indicators.note: the pieces are held inside the word for regard, which surrounds them

parts.note: to regard is to look at or see
DD is Doctor of Divinity, a cleric's degree

indicators.note: backed means turned back to front, so the copper symbol is read in reverse

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: An elderly Jewish man, a priest and a policeman supported him, all held in esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns CU (copper) into UC; A, DD and UC sit inside SEE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sadducees were a priestly Jewish party of the time of Jesus, so one is a Jew of ancient times.

clue.text: Given a half of bitter in a drinking-place, shut up!

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, so the half of bitter sits within the word for a pub

parts.note: an inn is a pub, a place to drink

indicators.note: a half of the word bitter means three of its six letters, here the back three

explanation.surface: Ordered a half-pint of bitter in the pub, someone is told to be quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a half of bitter' sounds like a half-pint order, but it is the back half of the word, TER, put in INN.
explanation.definitionFit: To intern someone is to confine or imprison them, especially in wartime, which is to shut them up.

clue.text: Club assessment is steep

parts.note: a mace is a heavy club used as a weapon
to rate is to assess; a rate is an assessment

explanation.surface: The golf club's valuation is excessive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steep' reads as an adjective, too high, but is the verb, to soak.
explanation.definitionFit: To macerate is to soften something by soaking it, which is to steep it.

clue.text: One hates to feel it

parts.note: read as a sad confession it is about an unpleasant feeling; read literally it describes what someone who hates feels

explanation.definitionFit: Enmity is hostility or hatred, the feeling of one who hates.

clue.text: A three-legged race?

parts.note: suggests the sports-day event, but race means a people, here one whose emblem is a three-legged symbol

explanation.walkthrough: The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, has a flag of three armoured legs joined at the hip.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man's flag shows three legs joined, so its people are the race with that emblem.

clue.text: Safe on strike in Wales

indicators.note: in an across clue one piece on another follows it, so the word for safe comes after

parts.note: to lam is to beat or thrash
peter is old criminal slang for a safe

explanation.surface: A secure workforce in Wales walks out on strike.
explanation.walkthrough: PETER is old underworld slang for a safe; LAMPETER is a small university town in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Lampeter is a town in Ceredigion, west Wales, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: A man named "X" occupied by monarch and church

indicators.note: the first piece is occupied by the second, which goes inside it

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A man called by a single letter, living with the Queen and the Church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'X' looks like an unknown name but is the Roman ten, TEN, with ER (the Queen) inside, then CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence is a man's first name, so it is what a man may be named.

clue.text: Dicky is curt when fruit is offered

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for weak or faulty, so the letters of is curt are disordered

explanation.surface: A rude reply when someone hands round fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name but is British slang for shaky or unsound, telling you to rearrange IS CURT.
explanation.definitionFit: Citrus is the family of fruits such as oranges, lemons and limes.

clue.text: The devious pieman uses the piper's son in children's entertainment

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, so the boy's name is set within the jumbled letters
something devious takes a winding course, so the word pieman is rearranged

parts.note: Tom, Tom, the piper's son is a nursery rhyme

explanation.surface: A scheming pie-seller employs a character from a nursery rhyme in a show for children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'devious' rearranges PIEMAN into PANIME, and TOM goes inside it. 'Tom, Tom, the piper's son' is a nursery rhyme, like 'Simple Simon met a pieman'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pantomime is the British Christmas theatre show for families, full of slapstick and songs.

clue.text: A minor machine part that's standard

indicators.note: part of the words minor machine is taken, a run of letters lying across them

explanation.surface: A small piece of machinery that is the usual kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part' signals that the answer lies inside 'minor machine', across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A norm is the usual or expected level, a standard.

clue.text: Don't work for others

definitions.meaning: to take a break and be idle

explanation.surface: Take a break and leave it to everybody else.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed solution's P is a misreading of R: both senses give a word meaning to relax and the remainder.
explanation.definitionFit: To rest is to stop working, and the rest are the remaining others.

clue.text: Pack round Tory leader, a properly-elected politician

indicators.note: a leader is the first, so only the opening letter of Tory is used

parts.note: an MP is a Member of Parliament, elected to the Commons

explanation.surface: A crowd gathers around the Conservative chief and a duly elected member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' takes just the T of Tory. To tamp is to pack earth or a charge down firmly round something.
explanation.definitionFit: To tamp is to ram down tightly, as when packing material round an explosive charge or a post.

clue.text: Plan in advance to make small change to back row

parts.note: p is a penny, a small coin
the rear is the back
a range is a row or line, as of mountains

explanation.surface: Scheme ahead to alter slightly the back row of seats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'small change' is P, a penny, not an instruction to alter something a little.
explanation.definitionFit: To prearrange is to fix the details beforehand, to plan ahead.

clue.text: Boys getting on in some craft

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, so the word on sits within the ship letters

parts.note: SS is steamship, a kind of craft at sea

explanation.surface: Lads make progress in a handicraft class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'craft' suggests a skill, but here it is a vessel, SS (steamship), with ON inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sons are male children, boys of their parents.

clue.text: The charge for converting men's assets

indicators.note: converting changes something into another form, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the possessive is taken with its S here as fodder letters

explanation.surface: A fee levied for turning men's possessions into cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'converting' rearranges MENS and ASSETS, ten letters in all, including the S of the possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: An assessment is an amount levied or charged, such as a tax rate.
